title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest leans on fresh 2026 evidence — long-awaited anti-aging RCTs landing with humble results, new women's HIIT and pelvic-floor trials, and updated sleep guidance. The cancer section covers integrative options and genetics to raise with an oncologist. Everything here is informational; talk to a clinician before acting on it.

sections.body:
This season's theme is **humility**: several long-awaited human trials of popular "longevity" compounds landed with modest or null results.

- **NMN (NAD+ booster).** A new 24-week RCT (adults 65+, 1,250 mg/day) in *npj Aging* confirmed NMN robustly **raises blood NAD+**, but found **no significant improvement** in the primary endpoint (hearing) or in physical performance. NAD+ went up; function didn't.
- **Urolithin A.** A 2026 systematic review of 5 RCTs (n=236) could only pool the 6-minute walk test and found a **directionally positive but statistically inconclusive** effect (low certainty). Strength/mitochondrial signals remain exploratory.
- **Rapamycin.** A review summarizing the **PEARL trial** (largest, 48 weeks, low intermittent dosing) notes it was **reasonably safe** but **missed** its visceral-fat endpoint; only modest, exploratory signals (muscle mass, self-reported pain in women).

Takeaway: prefer interventions with human RCTs, expect **small** effects, and be skeptical of single-pill longevity claims.

sources.title: Sustained NAD+ augmentation by high-dose nicotinamide mononucleotide supplementation in older adults: a 24-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
Effects of Urolithin A supplementation on muscle health outcomes in humans from randomized controlled trials
Geroprotective Effects of Drugs Modulating Metabolic Pathways: Perspectives of Pharmacology in Anti-Aging Therapy (PEARL rapamycin & taurine review)

sections.body:
New 2026 meta-analyses keep HIIT a **time-efficient** win for cardio fitness and body composition in women — with a clear nudge to **add strength work**.

- **Overweight/obese women.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* review of **15 RCTs** found HIIT significantly reduced body weight, BMI, **body-fat %**, and fat mass, and strongly improved **VO2max** (Hedges' g = 1.09). Effects on blood lipids were uncertain. (Certainty low to very low — expect real but modest gains.)
- **Recreationally active women.** A separate meta-analysis (15 studies) found **small VO2max gains** and lower **body-fat %**, but **no change** in overall body mass or fat mass — think recomposition, not the scale.
- **Midlife & older women.** A 2026 review (19 RCTs) showed HIIT reliably raises **VO2max** (high certainty) but does **little** for muscle strength or function on its own.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio and fat wins; **pair HIIT with resistance training** and progress gradually.

sources.title: Effects of HIIT on body composition, cardiorespiratory fitness, and selected lipid outcomes in adult women with overweight or obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Effects of HIIT on physical fitness and body composition in recreationally active females: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Effects of HIIT on cardiopulmonary fitness and physical function in middle-aged and elderly women: a systematic review and meta-analysis

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). The newest trials sharpen *how* to do it well.

- **PFMT beats Pilates.** An October 2026 RCT (105 women, *Int Urogynecol J*) compared targeted PFMT with Pilates (with or without pelvic-floor cueing). PFMT produced a far larger drop in incontinence impact (**ICIQ-SF −4.4 vs −0.7**) and bigger gains in muscle strength and squeeze pressure. Dedicated pelvic-floor work outperforms general core exercise.
- **Biofeedback helps a little.** A 2026 meta-analysis (8 RCTs) found adding **EMG biofeedback** to PFMT gives **small additional** improvements in symptoms, quality of life, and muscle strength — useful when you're unsure you're activating the right muscles.
- **Intensity + consistency matter.** A 99-woman postpartum RCT found a **high-intensity combined** protocol gave the best strength gains and the **lowest 6-month recurrence**.

Key point: **correct technique beats sheer reps** — confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback, and keep it consistent.

sources.title: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training Outperforms Pilates in Women with Stress Urinary Incontinence: A Randomized Controlled Trial

Effects of various pelvic floor muscle training forms and combined regimens on muscle strength, function, and recurrence rate in post-vaginal delivery SUI

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
Read "alternative" here as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard treatment** — never a replacement for HER2-targeted therapy. Two threads stand out.

- **Don't ignore vitamin D.** A 2026 retrospective study (*Nutrients*) of curative-intent HER2+ patients found that **failing to correct** a vitamin D deficiency carried a **~1.7× higher recurrence risk**, with a dose-response trend favoring higher levels. It echoes two 2025 RCTs where repletion **doubled** pathologic complete response (pCR) — and a prospective neoadjuvant RCT where vitamin D independently improved pCR (OR 2.33).
- **Genetics shape prognosis & drugs.** New 2026 data show **TP53 mutations predict shorter benefit** from trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) in metastatic HER2+ disease — yet preclinical work found **HER2;p53 co-mutated** tumors are especially sensitive to the TOP1-inhibitor payload, supporting a **neratinib + T-DXd** strategy now in early trials.

Important: much of this is **early or observational**. Use integrative options (like optimizing vitamin D) as *add-ons coordinated with your oncology team*, and ask about TP53/p53 testing — not as substitutes for standard care.

sources.title: Successful Vitamin D Replacement After Deficiency and Disease-Free Survival in Curative-Intent HER2+ Breast Cancer: A Retrospective Interventional Study
Vitamin D Supplementation During Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy for Breast Cancer Improves Pathological Complete Response: A Prospective Randomized Clinical Trial
HER2; p53 co-mutated cancers show increased histone acetylation and are sensitive to neratinib plus trastuzumab deruxtecan
Quantitative HER2 tissue and plasma profiling predicts the activity of trastuzumab deruxtecan for breast cancer (TP53 predicts outcome)

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance still puts **behavioral therapy first** and is honest about supplements.

- **CBT-I remains first-line.** A 2026 AASM clinical practice guideline on *combination* therapy made two conditional calls: CBT-I **plus** medication beats **medication alone**, but combination is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — the therapy itself does the heavy lifting, without drug risks. Digital CBT-I makes it more accessible.
- **Supplements, honestly.** A 2026 systematic review of RCTs concluded current evidence **does not support magnesium** as a routine insomnia treatment (benefits inconsistent, low certainty). AASM also **suggests against melatonin** for routine sleep-onset or maintenance insomnia — it's most useful for **circadian** issues like jet lag.
- **Newer medications.** **Orexin-receptor antagonists** (e.g., suvorexant; investigational seltorexant) improved sleep onset/maintenance in RCTs with fewer hangover effects than older Z-drugs — a clinician-guided option.

Every-night habits that help: keep a **fixed wake time**, reserve the bed **for sleep only**, dim lights and screens before bed, and if restless sleep persists, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I**.

sources.title: Combination treatment for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline
